5. Do not spend further submissions on outputs that have not passed all available pairs. Request another demo only if it can discriminate between specific remaining hypotheses.

## Common traps

- A solid row/column may be either a true separator or an edge/panel artifact. Confirm both sides are nonempty and determine orientation before slicing.
- “Foreground intersection” and “marker over background” can look plausible on a single demo but differ elsewhere. Compare full per-cell truth tables.
- Output color is not necessarily the source panel's background or the separator color. Derive it from consistent exact demo outputs.
- Dimension alignment and clipping are part of the rule; differing panel widths/heights should be handled explicitly.

# Repeated rejection workflow

A rejected submission falsifies the candidate transformation as a whole; it is not evidence that only one guessed color or coordinate needs adjustment. Preserve all complete demonstration input/output grids and compute the exact delta set for each. Keep hypotheses distinct and require full-grid equality against every fixture after each change. Never replace an unvalidated candidate with an identity or test-coordinate patch merely to use remaining attempts. A shape-valid program result is not semantic validation. Once demos are exhausted, make the best evidence-based inference from all recorded examples, but do not describe it as validated unless the complete fixture suite actually passes.

# Repeated-panel copying with crossing separators

This task class uses complete uniform separator lines to divide a grid into panels. The divider intersection means the vertical divider may not be uniform over the whole grid: test its color in rows outside the horizontal separator, and likewise test a horizontal divider outside vertical separators. Treat divider detection as independent from its crossing.

Infer the field background from the dominant color, partition into the resulting panels, and identify the panel with actual non-background pattern content. Copy its cell arrangement into each panel at matching relative coordinates, retaining separators and using background to pad when a destination extends beyond the source. If dimensions differ, avoid silently truncating or shifting: verify output sizes and cell-by-cell agreement across every demonstration.

An observed pair set can include an unchanged top panel and a lower source panel; this does not imply identity. Another pair may present a sparse source in one panel and show it tiled into every panel. Use all demos and exact array equality before submitting.

# Repeated-template anchor validation

For tasks that replicate a motif around marker cells, avoid inferring placement from the motif's bounding-box center. The visual marker may correspond to any specific template cell, and the copied object may be sparse or asymmetric.

## Procedure

1. List every non-background source cell with its color and coordinates, separately identifying target markers and any source anchor marker.
2. Test candidate anchor correspondences by translating the exact source-cell coordinate offsets to each target. Include orientation/reflection only when the demonstrations support it.
3. Determine whether target markers are consumed, retained, or overpainted, and whether the source motif remains unchanged.
4. Simulate each candidate on the full grid for every demonstration, including edge clipping and overlapping copies. Require exact dimensions and cell-by-cell equality before submitting.
5. Preserve demo fixtures as executable data when possible. After each code edit, rerun all fixtures and the test input through the task's actual transform function. A syntactically valid implementation or plausible printed output is not validation.

## Failure pattern to avoid

When several hypotheses have failed, don't keep changing an anchor offset based on intuition or replace the active implementation with an identity/placeholder and then submit guesses. Spend a remaining demo to discriminate hypotheses, and keep submissions strictly tied to fully validated code.

# Separator and panel-correspondence checks

Use when a grid seems split into aligned panels by a solid row or column.

- Do not assume the first uniform row/column is the divider. A single-panel noise pattern can itself contain a completely uniform row or column. Check candidate divider positions against the shape of the output and all demonstrations; true splits generally produce panels whose dimensions match the output convention.
- Verify each candidate's two sides have compatible dimensions before comparing coordinates. A divider can yield unequal widths; do not index beyond one panel, silently truncate, or invent a shift/reflection. Establish correspondence (same coordinate, reversed, overlap, etc.) from exact input/output fixtures first.
- Keep separator detection independent of palette-specific values where possible, but only after the evidence supports the structural criterion. Do not let an accidental uniform line take precedence over a known divider.
- Preserve complete demo fixtures and require exact output equality before submission. A plausible test answer is not evidence when the transform fails even one demo.

This session's concrete pitfall: a uniform internal row was mistaken for the separator in a vertical-panel puzzle, leading to an incorrect candidate panel shape and invalid pair indexing. The useful general lesson is dimensional and fixture-based separator validation, not the specific colors or coordinates.

# Separator and panel identification

A constant row or column is not automatically a divider: a uniform line can be part of a panel, and a full-color separator may occur in the middle rather than where a quick scan first finds a constant. Infer its structural role from the full grid, candidate panel dimensions, and output dimensions in all demonstrations.

For each plausible split, map coordinates from each panel to output and compare the complete foreground sets. This distinguishes copying one panel, filtering to a color, overlap, union, and mismatch/XOR. Preserve exact input/output fixtures before editing a task program; run exact whole-grid checks for every demo, not only a few rows or shapes. Do not test-submit until all available pairs pass.

Before requesting another example, articulate the competing rules it would distinguish. A demo request should resolve a real ambiguity, not substitute for reading the examples or debugging a speculative boundary choice.

# Demo economy when the rule is unclear

This note applies to new Continual-ARC instances with limited demo budgets.

## Evidence loop

1. Before requesting a pair, state internally at least two plausible rules and the observable difference that would separate them. Prefer a pair likely to test a structural condition (object identity, adjacency, repeated motif, orientation, or color-role mapping) rather than just provide another unrelated scene.
2. On receipt, record every changed cell and its before/after value, plus analogous unchanged cells. Distinguish object-level edits from grid-wide or color-wide edits.
3. Update or reject hypotheses immediately. If the pair does not distinguish candidates, do not request another on autopilot; refine the question so the next pair can do so.
4. Maintain complete executable fixtures. A candidate must reproduce every demo exactly before any submission. Test-run success, syntax validity, or agreement with a verbal summary is not validation.
5. When fixture capture or candidate testing is incomplete, say so operationally: do not submit a conjectural output as demonstrated. Avoid overwriting the task file repeatedly with identity functions or ad hoc heuristics.

## Failure pattern to avoid

Repeatedly requesting demos without extracting their deltas wastes the budget; then writing an untested rule after seeing many examples does not recover the evidence. Interleave analysis and validation with each new pair. If unresolved after the last useful demo, preserve the last supported program and follow the benchmark's action contract rather than fabricate certainty.

## Session-derived illustration

A sequence of varied sparse grids can each alter one localized object or marker in a different way. Superficial descriptions such as “small components are erased” may appear plausible on an early example but fail when later demos recolor a component instead. Track exact changed coordinates and compare object role/shape across *all* pairs before generalizing a color or size rule.

# Panel task validation after multiple demonstrations

This note records a reusable validation lesson from a stream instance involving horizontal and vertical panel separators.

- A solid separator can be a full row or column; detect orientation before splitting. A vertical separator example's output dimensions reflected one panel width, while another vertical case output matched the panels' shared width. Never assume output dimensions from orientation alone.
- Dominant colors are useful candidates for panel backgrounds, but output logic is not necessarily a foreground intersection or background coincidence. Compare exact demo outputs against candidate Boolean predicates over each panel's foreground masks and also inspect whether the output preserves a panel background or uses a third palette color.
- A rule that matches only a subset of demos is not validated. Build fixtures for all received pairs (including later demos that change orientation or palette), run the exact transform, and assert dimensions and every cell before submitting.
- Avoid trying speculative submissions after a failed verdict: the only feedback is binary, so it does not distinguish a wrong mask predicate from wrong output background, dimensions, or alignment. Spend remaining demos to discriminate these hypotheses, then revise and re-run the whole fixture suite.
- Keep the benchmark-required sequence: consult the task-id program first; if no usable validated program exists, request demos, implement and test, then submit only transform-produced output. Persist the final reproducing program after the verdict.

# Shape-aware translation: demo evidence and recovery lesson

This task's three demonstrations establish a translation selected by grid orientation, rather than a single fixed direction:

- 22x5 and 9x4 examples are taller than wide; every row after the first moves up one position, with the vacated final row filled with background.
- 3x19 is wider than tall; every row moves down one position, with the vacated first row filled with background.
- Thus the tested rule is: for `height > width`, shift rows upward; otherwise shift rows downward. Preserve dimensions and fill with the dominant background color.

Important recovery lesson: the existing task program's initial down-one-row rule passed neither tall-grid demo. Do not keep submitting the cached output after the first rejection. Request a demo, capture each complete fixture (including shape), compare row-wise changes, then revise. The first two demos independently reinforce upward translation for tall grids; the third distinguishes the orientation-dependent direction. Verify exact full-grid output on all fixtures before another submit.

Fixture constraints from the demonstrations:
- Demo 1: input 22x5, output 22x5; input row 7 is discarded, all other rows shift upward, final row is background.
- Demo 2: input 9x4, output 9x4; first all-background row is inserted, prior rows shift down.
- Demo 3: input 3x19, output 3x19; first all-background row is inserted, prior rows shift down.

These details are session-specific evidence; the reusable method is to infer translation direction from actual input/output coordinate deltas and test aspect-ratio hypotheses across all demos before submission.

# Sparse periodic-grid inference after rejection

This note captures a failure pattern from a sparse-grid instance with eight demos, mixed clue styles, and repeated binary rejections.

## What failed
- Treating different demonstration families as one visually similar rule without preserving fixtures. Demos included diagonal sparse marks, full-width horizontal stripes, and dense periodic outputs; they were not interchangeable evidence.
- Assuming a periodic fill direction from a single example. Row/column periodicity, `r+c` diagonal cycles, `r-c` diagonals, nearest-stripe extension, and row continuation all seemed plausible in isolation but lacked shared exact support.
- Rewriting the task program repeatedly with heuristics, then submitting despite not executing exact full-grid comparisons against every received pair. A program-generated grid is not a validated grid.
- Continuing submissions after multiple wrong verdicts without a materially changed hypothesis. Binary feedback only says the complete candidate is false; it does not point to a local coordinate or palette correction.
- Reusing the test grid as a fixed point merely because it visually appeared structured. No-op output is still a hypothesis and must be demonstrated.

## Correct recovery gate
1. Store every input/output pair as an executable fixture, not just verbal notes. Keep each complete matrix and assert dimensions/row widths.
2. For each pair, compute the exact changed-coordinate set. In uniform-row examples, record every row's input and output color; in sparse grids, record all occupied coordinates, colors, and lines containing repeated identical values.
3. Maintain candidate rules and their predictions across *all* pair types. Explicitly distinguish output that completes missing stripes from output that replaces or reorders existing stripes.
4. If no candidate predicts every cell of every demo, do not submit a speculative output. Use remaining demos only to resolve a named ambiguity; after the cap, stop inventing increasingly broad rules.
5. Only accept a transform after a script runs it on every fixture and asserts exact equality. Then run it on test, validate shape and value domain, and serialize precisely that result.

## Useful structural probes
For sparse diagonal-looking grids, group nonzero cells by `r+c` and `r-c`; report each line's value set and coordinates. This tests whether lines are truly monochromatic without assuming which family is the task's target. Check actual output deltas before assigning meaning to line direction. For row-stripe demos, list full-width nonzero rows and compare exact output sequence, including unchanged clue rows and newly filled rows.

## Decision discipline under a depleted budget
After one rejected attempt, prefer a demo over a second speculative submission when demos remain. After several wrong submissions, only spend another attempt when the new candidate is materially different and fully supported by fixtures. Do not interpret frustration or missing execution as evidence for a rule.

See also `continual-arc-solving` for the required program-first workflow and exact final action protocol.

# Sparse frame-highlight lesson

When demonstrations show sparse foreground marks and recolor selected background cells to a third color, compare the changed coordinates across all pairs before implementing. A useful candidate to test is the outline of the foreground bounding box: recolor only background cells on its top, bottom, left, or right edges, leaving existing foreground marks and all interior cells unchanged. Do not assume this rule merely because it fits one example; some outputs may indicate a different subset of outline points.

Validate the candidate on every received pair by exact whole-grid comparison, then run it on the test input. In this session, repeated speculative rewrites and one-off test-only executions failed to validate the hypothesis against complete demonstrations. Maintain a single explicit candidate and use each new demo to resolve ambiguity.

# Sparse line/frame inference after rejection

## Evidence protocol

- Retain each complete demo as an executable input/output fixture. Never substitute a handwritten summary or partial geometry for a full grid.
- Compute and inspect the full delta, including all original non-background marks and analogous untouched coordinates. Verify exact dimensions and row widths.
- Test every competing geometric interpretation against every demo before applying it to the test.

## Distinguishing mechanics

Sparse points may depict endpoints of lines, fragments of a frame, or a more selective motif. Do not infer that every pair of marks in a row/column should be connected. Check whether the output adds only frame edges, fills selected segments, or propagates another pattern; explicitly compare predicted additions with unchanged cells. Preserve input markers and their values unless output evidence establishes recoloring or replacement. Demos with different aspect ratios, orientations, and palettes are particularly useful for separating an invariant geometric rule from accidental color/count cues.

## After a rejected submission

A rejection invalidates the entire hypothesis. Preserve the prior program while building exact fixtures; avoid successive speculative file rewrites or test-only output generation. Request a further example when a named ambiguity remains and the new pair could resolve it. Submit only after a single general transform reproduces all complete demos by exact grid equality.

# Sparse geometry and incorrect verdicts

## Recovery discipline

An incorrect submission is evidence against the task hypothesis, not merely a likely typo. Do not repeat the same generated grid or perform superficial edits while retaining the same rule. Reconstruct each demonstration's exact changed cells and spatial relations, then identify what the hypothesis fails to explain. If plausible interpretations remain and demos are available, request one that discriminates between them.

Keep every input/output pair as a fixture. Before submitting again, run the current task transform against every complete pair and compare exact dimensions and every cell. A transform merely running on the test input is not validated. Submit exactly the result generated by the validated program.

## Sparse line-art / fragmented frame tasks

A visually plausible bounding rectangle can be a false generalization. Some boundary gaps may be intentionally left untouched, even when other gaps on the apparent same outline are highlighted. Before adopting a frame-completion rule, verify both positive and negative locations across demos with varied placements, shapes, and orientations. Explain why selected pixels change and why analogous gaps do not.

Avoid iterative speculative rewrites without fixture execution. Maintain one explicit hypothesis at a time; use exact demo validation to reject or refine it before spending a submission.

# Recovering from a rejected sparse-grid transform

A cached program can execute correctly and still encode the wrong transformation. A wrong verdict invalidates the rule; it is not evidence for a small coordinate tweak.

## Coordinate-led validation

1. Preserve the complete demo input and output, including dimensions and every background cell.
2. List all non-background coordinates in both grids. Compare their coordinate sets and test whether output marks correspond to input marks under one uniform offset, reflection, crop, or other global spatial operation.
3. Confirm the candidate against every cell, not just the visible mark cluster. In particular, identify which rows/columns become vacated and whether marks are clipped at boundaries.
4. Implement the general operation and execute it on every available demo. Require exact grid equality before generating and submitting the test result.
5. On rejection, request a discriminating demo instead of submitting another unvalidated guess.

In the demonstrated vertical-shift pattern, the output foreground coordinates were precisely the input foreground coordinates shifted down one row, with top row vacated and bottom overflow clipped. The example was verified across the full grid; do not assume that rule for unrelated tasks without evidence.

# Sparse patterns around separator lines

After a cached transform is rejected, reassess whether a full-length line is a boundary or marker rather than assuming the cached program's interpretation. Distinguish separator color from background and locate the active pattern's full spatial extent, including isolated cells. A transformation may mark a row or column just beyond the pattern's far edge, rather than immediately adjacent to the separator or one salient object. Validate the interpretation against the complete demo output before applying it to the test. Test-only execution is not evidence of correctness: require exact full-grid agreement on all available demos. If plausible interpretations remain, request a discriminating demo rather than submit another unvalidated variation.

# Validate the actual submission payload

Before a benchmark submit action, check both the transform output and the JSON grid being sent. The action payload must contain exactly the input's intended output dimensions: `len(grid)` rows, each `len(row)` equal to the intended width, integer values in 0–9. A mismatch between a valid program result and the manually composed action can invalidate the answer even when the intended transformation is otherwise correct. Prefer using the exact transform-produced grid and verify row count and widths immediately before submitting.

After a wrong verdict, distinguish a malformed-grid rejection from a valid-but-wrong answer. A message that explicitly says the grid was not valid ARC grid points first to payload dimensions/format, so audit that before revising the visual rule. If the verdict says simply incorrect, treat it as evidence against the transform hypothesis. When demos are exhausted, do not cycle through identical outputs; avoid ungrounded guesses and use only distinct hypotheses supported by the observed pairwise differences.

# Tool economy and demo-fixture validation

This note arose from an ARC stream run where repeated file checks and unrelated skill/reference/tool calls consumed turns without advancing the puzzle. The task program was eventually written and executed on the test, but the demos were never encoded as complete fixtures and exact outputs were never compared; a working transform call is not evidence of a validated rule.

## Reliable practice

1. Perform the required task-file check once at instance start. If absent, do not repeat it unless something changed the file state.
2. Treat each demonstration as a full input/output constraint. Capture complete grids in a reproducible fixture (for example, a small Python test harness), then run the actual task module's `transform` against every fixture and assert equal dimensions and every cell.
3. Do not submit on the strength of a plausible interpretation, a syntax check, or merely seeing that `transform(test_grid)` runs. If demos remain and the rule is unresolved, use a request for a demonstration that distinguishes live hypotheses.
4. Keep tool actions focused on the required program, fixture validation, and test-output generation. Avoid empty commands, repeated file existence checks, and reference loads that do not address an active inference issue.
5. Only submit the exact test grid emitted by the fully demo-validated task program. After verdict, follow the required persistence/finish sequence.

## Pitfall

A hand-constructed approximation of a large demo is not a fixture: omitted cells and transcription errors can silently give false confidence. Preserve the exact complete arrays or use a parser from the original demo text, and compare full matrices.

# Turn economy when the protocol is strict

In benchmark conversations requiring exactly one action JSON on every turn, minimize auxiliary tool calls. Once the task program has been checked and found absent, stop repeating file existence checks and focus on analyzing the demonstrations already provided. Reload only the specific reference needed for a live reasoning issue; don't repeatedly retrieve already-current references. Choose a demo request because it distinguishes an explicit pair of competing hypotheses, not as a reflex after every new demo. Keep the final response to the required action object, with no extra prose.

This is a process-efficiency lesson, not a substitute for the benchmark's required correctness workflow: implement `transform`, verify it exactly against every available pair, submit only its produced test output, and persist the validated task program after verdict.

# Persisting validated task programs

A solved submission and a correct reusable program are separate deliverables. After the verdict, persist the rule that was actually demonstrated and tested—not an approximate shortcut inferred late in the instance.

## Checklist

1. Derive the transformation from the demos: identify the seed object/shape, background and target colors, and how candidate placements are selected.
2. Implement a general `transform(grid)` using relationships that hold across the examples; avoid relying on fixed demo color numbers or assuming a palette that only fits one test.
3. Execute the exact implementation against every received demo pair and assert full grid equality, including dimensions. If demo fixtures were not retained as complete matrices, reconstruct them before asserting that the file reproduces all demos.
4. Execute the same implementation on the test input and confirm it produces the grid submitted.
5. Only then save or replace `programs/<task id>.py`. A post-verdict requirement to save does not excuse writing an untested or contradictory implementation; do not claim it reproduces demos unless verified.

## Pitfall

A late speculative code file can be inconsistent with the reasoning or output that earned a correct verdict. Review the saved file for stale variables, palette assumptions, and behavior on all examples before finishing.

# Validation pitfalls in continual ARC instances

A file write, syntax check, or plausible visual interpretation does not establish a correct transformation. For every available demonstration, construct the input grid in a reproducible fixture, run the task's `transform`, and compare dimensions and every cell with the provided output. Only submit the grid actually returned by that validated program.

For stamp-copy tasks, establish the anchor from evidence (for example, the marker aligned to a distinctive stamp pixel), exact orientation, and whether cells matching the background or intermediate fill color are part of the copied stamp. Preserve overlap semantics by applying copies in a deterministic order. Check edge clipping against the grid bounds and ensure original markers/stamp are handled as the rule dictates.

After receiving another demonstration, re-run the current candidate against all accumulated pairs before submitting. If it fails, revise the hypothesis and code; do not issue speculative submissions or manually invent outputs. Keep experimentation focused in the task-id program and a minimal test harness instead of repeatedly overwriting with placeholders or creating unrelated temporary files.

# Value-level panel-rule diagnosis

When a grid is split into aligned panels by a solid row or column, do not assume the output is a generic foreground intersection or that it reproduces an input panel. Record output dimensions, fill color, highlight color, and exact changed coordinates for every example.

A useful candidate family is aligned value predicates: same exact color in both panels, equal background cells, equal foreground cells, or asymmetric background/foreground combinations. For each candidate, evaluate it over every aligned cell and compare the complete predicted output, including fill/background palette and dimensions. Use color-frequency counts only to hypothesize backgrounds; do not let a mode-based assumption override contradictory demonstrations.

Before submitting, use fixtures containing all accumulated demos and run the task transform. Assert complete-grid equality, not just marker coordinates. When a new demo changes panel orientation or palette, revisit the whole rule and verify all prior cases; do not patch with task-specific exceptions. A failed binary submission cannot identify whether the mismatch was predicate, palette, or dimensions, so maximize information from demos before spending attempts.
